source.title: Deriving Scaling Laws for OpenEuroLLM Models: Learning Rate, Batch Size and Loss
source.authors: Niccolò Ajroldi; Diana-Alexandra Onutu; Haider Al-Tahan; J. Franke; Sampo Pyysalo; J. Jitsev; Aaron Klein

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and table rows are flattened or imperfectly rendered, but the main results and fit metrics are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures loss scaling on its own model and data sweeps, tests held-out extrapolation, and finds that the separable Chinchilla form misses an N–D interaction while an interaction model fits better.
record.gate_note: The study also reports extensive optimal learning-rate and batch-size results; these are not rows because they do not measure the claim's parameter/token compute-optimal allocation. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as findings here.
record.test_reason: The study fits loss laws to its own 47M–1.7B dense LM sweeps (Nemotron-CC, up to 300BT). It shows the separable Chinchilla form misfits extreme N/D and extrapolates poorly to a held-out 1.7B model, while an N–D interaction (Skaling) form fits and extrapolates better. That is a specific argument that the standard form needs restating (V1, V7), plus a small-range extrapolation test (V2). It also plots downstream error against compute (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the separable Chinchilla law poorly captures their range of training regimes and that the Skaling N–D coupling extrapolates better to held-out 1.7B points. They say small-scale laws extrapolated over roughly an order of magnitude, but holding at much larger scales is unclear and compute-optimal scaling needs further analysis. They add that downstream error falls consistently with compute. The paper's main focus is optimal LR and batch-size scaling and annealing effects.
record.recipe_differences: Measures validation cross-entropy across dense OpenEuroLLM models and token budgets and fits Chinchilla-style and interaction-based scaling forms. Uses its own WSD pretraining setup, Nemotron-CC data, Huber fitting, and held-out 1.7B model; it does not reproduce the original studies' full-scale compute-optimal parameter/token allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted relationship depends on the functional form: the separable Chinchilla fit misses an N–D interaction, while the Skaling interaction form fits better. The authors also state that exponents reported across studies vary with datasets, architectures, and training configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: Jointly optimal batch size and learning rate scale as power laws in N and D: b*∝N^0.145 D^0.46 and η*∝N^-0.417 D^0.086. These laws are validated on the held-out 1.7B model (MAPE 10–37%), and conditional optima have their own laws.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal learning rate and batch size follow predictable power laws in model size and token budget.

fits_no_version.finding: The loss gain from WSD annealing (ΔL) is not constant: it varies with N, D, η and b, and the optimal LR shifts up to ~4× between the stable and decay phases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LR-annealing gains and hyperparameter optima depend on scale and configuration, so constant-LR checkpoints are not a constant-offset proxy for scaling-law fits.

record.problems: The model range is limited to 47 million–1.7 billion parameters and the authors say substantially larger-scale extrapolation is unclear. The loss fit compares a separable form with one interaction form, and compute-optimal scaling needs further analysis. Some displayed downstream results are figure-only.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant reported results were left out. Extensive optimal learning-rate and batch-size findings were excluded because they do not test the listed parameter/token compute-optimal allocation claim.

untested.parts: Power law over several orders of magnitude: N spans ~1.5 orders (47M–1.7B), D ~1.7 orders (6–300BT). Single-variable laws with the other factors non-bottleneck are not isolated.
Prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger; the held-out model is under 2× the largest training model.
Untested entirely: no N_opt(C) or D_opt(C) exponents are reported.
Untested: shape covaries with size, with no fixed-N comparison.
Untested: text pretraining only, with no repeated data, other modalities, fine-tuning or transfer.
Quantitative predictability (a fitted downstream law, or prediction from pretraining loss).
Variation of parameter-counting convention, schedule, dataset or fitting method. Only two functional forms are compared.

missing.what: Fitted exponents for both forms: Chinchilla α=0.2807, β=0.2534, E=1.418; Skaling α=0.3496, β=0.491, E=1.03, k=0.41, with bootstrap SEs. These are needed to compare exponents across studies (V7).

record.verdict_notes: Several of the reader's labels were wrong and are corrected here. The Chinchilla misfit was labelled 'challenges' for V1 and V7, but it qualifies V1's form (limits_scope) and supports V7. The V2 limits_scope on larger scales was really an untested part and is moved to untested. r2 should not link to V2. r5 is a derived curve, not independent evidence. No original source is involved. The authors' remark that exponents vary across studies is cited and is not a result here.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not isolate one-variable power laws while ensuring the other two quantities are non-bottlenecks, or establish the claim across several orders of magnitude.
The largest held-out model is 1.7B parameters; prediction at models orders of magnitude larger is not tested.
The study derives compute-optimal loss, but does not report how the loss-minimizing parameter count and token count individually scale with compute.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns English-prevalent text pretraining and does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream error is plotted against compute; the study does not test a quantitative prediction from pretraining loss to downstream performance.

The study compares separable and interaction-based loss forms, but does not systematically vary fitting method, schedule, dataset, or parameter-count convention, nor test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.

rows.subject: OpenEuroLLM dense models (aggregate scaling fit; training models 0.048B–0.98B)
rows.size_stated: 47 million to 1.7 billion parameters overall; fit uses training models up to 0.98B
rows.operation_detail: Fit the Chinchilla form L(N,D) = E + AN^-α + BD^-β to validation loss.

conditions.value: intermediate N and D observations; extremes also assessed

rows.measure: Fit quality (Huber loss); the authors state the form fits intermediate values satisfactorily but systematically underperforms at extreme N or D and shows N–D interaction in residuals.
rows.uncertainty: Bootstrap standard errors are reported for fitted parameters; no uncertainty stated for this fit-quality comparison.
rows.note: The reported residual pattern is that residuals increase with D for small models and decrease with D for large models, indicating a non-separable N–D relationship.
rows.check: The Chinchilla misfit at extreme N/D (Huber 1.76e-04 vs 3.66e-05), with N–D interaction in the residuals, is fully observed for V7 (the form choice matters and the curve bends from the separable law). For V1 it reads as partial: the separable sum of power laws holds only at intermediate N/D. It is mirrored by r2.

source_check.correct: The fit includes the training grid, including extreme N/D observations; satisfactory fit, rather than fitting-data selection, is confined to intermediate values. State: observed for V7; cannot_determine for V1's bottleneck-free conditional power laws over several orders of magnitude.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5, Figure 10a, Table 3; Appendix C, Equation 15.
source_check.problem: The fitting range is misstated, and joint-form misspecification does not establish the state of V1.

rows.subject: OpenEuroLLM dense models (aggregate scaling fit; Skaling form)
rows.size_stated: 47 million to 1.7 billion parameters overall; fit uses training models up to 0.98B
rows.operation_detail: Fit the Skaling loss form with an interaction exponent coupling model and data capacity.
rows.measure: Fit quality (Huber loss) and estimated interaction exponent
rows.value: Skaling fit: Huber loss 3.66e-05; estimated interaction exponent ∼0.41 (Table 3 gives 0.4105)
rows.uncertainty: Table 3 reports bootstrap standard errors; the interaction exponent is 0.4105 ± 0.033.
rows.note: The authors report better fits, particularly at extreme grid observations, for the interaction form.
rows.check: This is an in-sample training fit, not extrapolation, so V2 should be removed. The held-out test is in r4.

source_check.correct: Skaling Huber loss = 3.66e-05; interaction exponent = 0.4105. State: observed for V7; cannot_determine for V1's conditional power laws over several orders of magnitude.
source_check.problem: The coupled joint fit establishes functional-form sensitivity but does not directly establish the full V1 claim.

rows.subject: OpenEuroLLM dense models (held-out 1.7B model; Chinchilla prediction)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate the fitted Chinchilla loss law on held-out 1.7B-model observations.
rows.note: The text says the Chinchilla form poorly extrapolates to the held-out 1.7B model.
rows.check: Extrapolation is only from ≤0.98B to 1.7B (<2× in N), far short of the 'orders of magnitude' V2 names. Chinchilla's held-out RMSE is 0.0174, about 3× Skaling's.

source_check.correct: State: observed for V7's functional-form dependence; cannot_determine for V2's orders-of-magnitude extrapolation. The largest fitting model is 983.1M parameters and the held-out model is 1.713B.
source_check.problem: Partial conflates observed form sensitivity with an extrapolation distance that V2 specifies but this test does not cover.

rows.subject: OpenEuroLLM dense models (held-out 1.7B model; Skaling prediction)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate the fitted Skaling loss law on held-out 1.7B-model observations.
rows.note: The authors describe the Skaling form as accurately extrapolating to the held-out 1.7B points.
rows.check: Observed only within a small extrapolation range (0.98B→1.7B; the authors say roughly an order of magnitude, presumably in compute).

source_check.correct: State: observed for V7; cannot_determine for V2's orders-of-magnitude extrapolation. Accurate held-out prediction is demonstrated only from a fitting grid extending through 983.1M to a 1.713B model.
source_check.problem: Successful prediction at the modest tested gap does not establish V2's specified extrapolation distance.

rows.subject: OpenEuroLLM dense models (compute-optimal loss curve derived from fitted Skaling form)
rows.operation_detail: Derive the minimum loss over N and D under compute allocation C from the fitted functional form.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal validation loss as a function of compute
rows.uncertainty: Bootstrap mean estimate; no interval stated for this curve.
rows.note: The curve is derived from the fitted form; the authors say further analysis is needed to characterize compute-optimal scaling and extrapolation to unseen scales.
rows.check: L*(C) is derived analytically from the fitted Skaling form, not measured separately. Its power-law shape follows from the fit, so it cannot independently confirm V1. It gives no N_opt/D_opt, so it does not bear on V3.

rows.subject: OpenEuroLLM models (aggregate; per-(N,D) lowest-validation-loss configurations)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate downstream performance on DCLM-CORE and plot downstream error against training compute.
rows.measure: Downstream performance error versus training compute
rows.value: Figure only; the text states downstream error consistently decreases as compute increases across model scales.
rows.note: The text also says the smallest model's error plateaus quickly as additional tokens provide diminishing gains, while larger models continue to benefit from more compute.
rows.check: Figure-only. Error decreases with compute, but the smallest model plateaus. No fitted law or loss-to-downstream prediction is reported.
